fields.origins: Native to eastern and south-eastern Australia. The name moluccanus comes from a mistaken type locality, and the bird is not native to the Moluccas. Former subspecies such as the Red-collared Lorikeet are now treated as separate species. Feral populations are established around Perth and in Auckland. IUCN lists Australia as the native country and also records an introduced resident population.
fields.distribution: From Cape York and north-eastern Queensland south through New South Wales and Victoria to south-eastern South Australia, including Kangaroo Island. Birds of the World calls Tasmanian birds vagrants. Birds in Backyards says the species is becoming more common in Tasmania, and the World Parrot Trust includes Tasmania in the range. Birds are largely sedentary, with local movements to flowering trees.
fields.habitat: Rainforest, open forest, woodland, heath, mangroves and urban parks and gardens, especially where eucalypts are flowering. Birds of the World says it favours edges and disturbed vegetation.
fields.breeding: In southern Australia the season is August to January on Wikipedia and June to January on Birds in Backyards. Eggs are laid on wood dust in a tree hollow, usually a eucalypt, and only the female incubates. Birds in Backyards gives a clutch of 2 and incubation of 23 days, with a nestling period of 45 days. Wikipedia gives 1–3 eggs and incubation of around 25 days. Other accounts put fledging at about 7–9 weeks. Both parents feed the young.
fields.diet: Mainly nectar and pollen, taken with a brush-tipped tongue, plus fruit, seeds and some insects. Birds in Backyards says the species has benefited from flowering garden plants and from artificial feeding.
fields.threats: It is common and has increased in eastern cities, and it is treated as a pest in Perth. The 2024 IUCN text still says the population is suspected to be decreasing because of unsustainable exploitation. That global sentence conflicts with the Australian accounts of abundance. Competition for hollows is mentioned in secondary accounts and is not quantified on the pages read here.
fields.size: Birds in Backyards, still under the older name Trichoglossus haematodus, gives 28–32 cm, average 30 cm, and about 133 g. Other accounts give 25–30 cm or about 26 cm, and published weights run from about 75 g to 157 g.
fields.conservation: Least Concern, assessed 15 January 2024. The IUCN trend text says Decreasing, and the decline is not treated as fast enough to approach Vulnerable. The same page says the Action Plan for Australian Birds 2020 did not find it near threatened. It is not on the EPBC threatened-fauna list extracted 28 August 2026. It is not named in the bird tables retrieved from the June 2024 and March 2025 Victorian FFG lists. The DEECA page records one July 2026 amendment, the plant Hibbertia porcata. The July 2026 PDF and spreadsheet returned HTTP 403. Birds in Backyards marks the federal status Secure. Parrots, including this species on the World Parrot Trust page, are on CITES Appendix II.

conflicts: Tasmania: Birds of the World, vagrant; Birds in Backyards, becoming more common; World Parrot Trust, included in the range; IUCN population text, rare in Tasmania, citing del Hoyo et al. 1997.
Southern season: Birds in Backyards June–January; Wikipedia August–January. Outside the south, breeding is recorded in every month except March.
Clutch: Birds in Backyards 2; Wikipedia and several other accounts 1–3; World Parrot Trust 2–3.
Incubation: Birds in Backyards 23 days; Wikipedia around 25 days; one aviculture account 23–25 days; one secondary account 25–26 days.
Nestling period: Birds in Backyards 45 days; other accounts about 7–9 weeks or 54–57 days.
Length: Birds in Backyards 28–32 cm; Birdfact 25–30 cm; World Parrot Trust 26 cm.

sources.title: Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve – Biodiversity & Trails
sources.supports: Dominant trees are Manna Gum (Eucalyptus viminalis) and River Red Gum (Eucalyptus camaldulensis). The predominant large shrub is Hedge Wattle (Acacia paradoxa), which forms prickly thickets. Areas of Banksia and Sheoak are present. The ground layer is dominated by Wallaby Grass. The reserve is about 1,050 ha of grassy woodland between Inverleigh and Teesdale. The page says 119 bird species have been recorded there, and that bats, gliders and possums use tree hollows. It does not name a nest tree for any bird in this batch.

sources.title: Wild plants of Inverleigh — Recreating the Country
sources.supports: Lawson's Tree is a River Red Gum, and many River Red Gums grow along the Leigh River and on the local plains. The local mix named on the page includes Golden Wattle, Black Wattle, Blackwood, Lightwood, Hedge Wattle, Black Sheoak, Drooping Sheoak and Silver Banksia. Sweet Bursaria is described as now quite rare in the local bushland. The Nature Conservation Reserve is the old Inverleigh Common, about 1,000 ha, three kilometres north of town. A spring list for the reserve includes Kangaroo Grass and Supple Spear Grass. Yellow Box is not named on this page.

sources.title: Plains and Rivers Planting Guide — Golden Plains Shire
sources.supports: The southern part of the shire was open grassland of Kangaroo, Wallaby and Spear grasses, with open grassy woodland of scattered River Red Gum, Drooping She-oak and, on fertile ground, Manna Gum. River valleys held River Red Gum and Blackwood. The species table lists River Red Gum and Manna Gum for plains and rivers, Yellow Box and Yellow Gum and Drooping She-oak and Golden Wattle and Silver Banksia for plains, and Sweet Bursaria for plains and rivers. This is a planting list for the shire, not a survey of which of those plants stand inside the Inverleigh reserve.

sources.title: Rainbow Lorikeet — Birds in Backyards
sources.supports: The live page uses the older name Trichoglossus haematodus. Wide range of treed habitats, including rainforest, woodland and well-treed urban areas. Nectar and pollen from flowers of shrubs or trees, plus fruit, seeds and some insects. Eggs on chewed decayed wood, usually in a hollow limb of a eucalypt. References include HANZAB volume 4. The Trichoglossus moluccanus URL returned 404.

sources.title: Rainbow Lorikeet — Australian Museum
sources.supports: Classification on the page is Trichoglossus moluccanus. Same habitat as Birds in Backyards: treed habitats including rainforest, woodland and well-treed urban areas. References Higgins 1999, HANZAB volume 4.

sources.title: Rainbow lorikeet — Wikipedia
sources.supports: Diet is mainly fruit, pollen and nectar. Eucalypt nectar is important in Australia. Other nectar sources named include Pittosporum and Grevillea, and the account also lists garden fruit. Nests in hollows of tall trees such as eucalypts, and also palm trunks or overhanging rock. In southern Australia breeding is usually August to January.

rainbow-lorikeet.trees: Rainbow Lorikeets feed on nectar and pollen in flowering trees and nest in a eucalypt hollow. The live Birds in Backyards page is still filed as Trichoglossus haematodus. It says they use a wide range of treed habitats, including well-treed suburbs, lay eggs on chewed decayed wood in a hollow limb of a eucalypt, and take nectar and pollen plus fruit, seeds and some insects. The Australian Museum uses the name Trichoglossus moluccanus and gives the same habitat. Wikipedia lists eucalypt nectar as important in Australia, and also Pittosporum, Grevillea and garden fruit. Manna Gum and River Red Gum are the local eucalypts that flower. Which street or garden trees on High Street the birds use is not documented. An ALA query for Trichoglossus haematodus inside 5 km returned 0 records. The 56 records are under Trichoglossus moluccanus.
rainbow-lorikeet.hangouts: Within 5 km of Inverleigh, the Atlas of Living Australia holds 56 records of this species. They cluster in town and on the Leigh: Lawson Reserve (14), the Leigh River south of the Hamilton Highway (9), High Street (7), the Leigh River north of the highway (4) and the Barwon–Leigh junction (3). Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve has 4 under that label, and only 1 on the Old Shelford Track string. The Inverleigh Recreation Reserve has 2, and the Leigh downstream of Lawson Reserve has 2. One string is only the words river walk, with 1 record. This is a thin sample beside the other parrots.

fields.origins: Native to south-eastern Australia and endemic there. The current scientific name is Zanda funerea. Calyptorhynchus funereus is the synonym still used on some Australian pages. IUCN lists Australia as the only native country.
fields.distribution: From south and central-eastern Queensland through New South Wales and Victoria to the Eyre Peninsula, Kangaroo Island and Tasmania, including Bass Strait islands. BirdLife gives Eyre Peninsula to south and central-eastern Queensland. Inverleigh sits in the southern Victorian part of that range. Movements are poorly known; non-breeding birds wander in small flocks.
fields.habitat: Eucalypt forest and woodland, coastal heath and pine plantations, from the coast into the ranges. Nesting depends on large hollows in old eucalypts.
fields.breeding: The season changes with latitude. Birds of the World gives October to March in South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania, and earlier months farther north. The Western Volcanic Plains guide, for country near Inverleigh, gives November to February. The nest is a large hollow lined with wood chips. The clutch is two, and usually only one chick is raised. The female incubates and the male feeds her. A local Bellarine guide says incubation is around four weeks. A secondary profile says about 29 days. Birds in Backyards does not print a day count. The young remain with the parents for about six months.
fields.diet: Seeds of banksias, hakeas, she-oaks and eucalypts, seeds pulled from pine cones, and wood-boring insect larvae. BirdLife says the favoured food is seeds of native trees and pine cones, with some insects. One secondary account says the southern birds eat seeds only and the eastern birds also take grubs. That split is not in the BirdLife text.
fields.threats: Loss and fragmentation of forest, and the loss of old hollow-bearing trees, are the threats named by BirdLife, the Australian Wildlife Conservancy and Wikipedia. Wikipedia says numbers are declining in Victoria and South Australia even though birds can be plentiful near pine plantations. On the Eyre Peninsula the birds now rely on Aleppo pine after sugar-gum woodland was broken up. Hollows are also lost to other birds, possums and feral honeybees in secondary accounts. The species was shot as an orchard pest in parts of New South Wales until the 1940s. The 2024 IUCN text says the global population is suspected to be stable and at least 25,000 birds.
fields.size: 55–65 cm. Birds in Backyards gives an average of 60 cm and about 700 g. Australian Geographic gives 750–900 g. The two weight ranges do not match.
fields.conservation: Least Concern, assessed 15 January 2024, with the trend stated as stable and the population put at least at 25,000 birds. The justification says there is no evidence for declines or substantial threats, which conflicts with regional reports of decline in Victoria and South Australia. It is not on the EPBC threatened-fauna list extracted 28 August 2026, and a SPRAT search for cockatoos does not list Zanda funerea among the threatened cockatoos. South Australia lists it as Vulnerable. The Western Volcanic Plains guide says it is not listed under the Victorian FFG Act, and it is not named in the bird tables retrieved from the June 2024 and March 2025 FFG lists. The DEECA page records one July 2026 amendment, the plant Hibbertia porcata. The July 2026 PDF and spreadsheet returned HTTP 403. A 2023 taxonomic review argues that the eastern, southern-mainland and Tasmanian birds are three species. IUCN and BirdLife still treat one species, Zanda funerea, with three subspecies.

conflicts: Breeding season in the south: Birds of the World, October–March in South Australia, Victoria and Tasmania; Western Volcanic Plains guide, November–February; a secondary account, July–January in the south and March–August in the north.
Incubation: Bellarine community guide, around four weeks; a secondary species profile, about 29 days. Birds in Backyards prints no figure. The HANZAB account was not retrieved.
Weight: Birds in Backyards about 700 g; Australian Geographic 750–900 g.

Global trend against local reports: IUCN 2024, stable, in the absence of evidence for declines or substantial threats; BirdLife cites a significant east-coast decline in State of Australia’s Birds 2015; Wikipedia says the species is declining in Victoria and South Australia.

Diet of southern birds: BirdLife includes some insects across the species; one secondary account says Tasmanian, western Victorian and South Australian birds eat seeds only.

sources.supports: A direct fetch did not return the article body. Indexed search text says Manna Gums have sugary leaf deposits favoured by birds, River Red Gums prefer moist gullies and hold hollows used by birds, Hedge Wattle shelters small birds, and female Drooping Sheoak cones are a favourite with cockatoos and parrots. sources.title: Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoo — Birds in Backyards
sources.supports: The live page is filed as Calyptorhynchus funereus. The Zanda funerea URL returned 404. Favours eucalypt woodland and pine plantations. Seeds of native trees and pine cones, seeds of ground plants, and some insects. Nest is a large tree hollow lined with wood chips. References are field guides, not HANZAB.

sources.title: Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoo — Australian Museum
sources.supports: The page still classifies the bird as Calyptorhynchus funereus. Same habitat and feeding summary as Birds in Backyards: eucalypt woodland and pine plantations, native seeds and pine cones.

sources.title: Yellow-tailed black cockatoo — Wikipedia
sources.supports: Prefers native temperate forests and is also in pine plantations. Breeding needs large old trees. Nests in large vertical hollows of tall trees, generally eucalypts. Roosts in tall emergent eucalypts. The feeding account names she-oaks including Allocasuarina verticillata, Banksia including B. marginata, Acacia, Hakea, and introduced Pinus radiata and Cupressus torulosa. Also wood-boring larvae.

sources.title: Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoo — BirdLife Australia
sources.supports: Scientific name on the page is Zanda funerea. Once fed on seeds of banksias, hakeas and casuarinas, and on insect larvae in wattle branches. Monterey Pine cones are now a frequent food. Habitat tags on the page are woodland and forest. The feeding and breeding blocks on the fetched page match the Birds in Backyards account: native seeds and pine cones, and a large tree hollow lined with wood chips.

sources.title: Funeral Rites — BirdLife Australia
sources.supports: Describes birds feeding in a pine, tearing cones apart, and says the older foods were banksias, hakeas and she-oaks. Monterey Pine plantations since the 1920s shifted much of the feeding onto exotic conifers. Eucalypts form the hollows pines in plantations do not. The scene is not located at Inverleigh.

yellow-tailed-black-cockatoo.trees: Yellow-tailed Black-Cockatoos feed on hard native seeds and pine cones, and they nest in a large eucalypt hollow. Birds in Backyards and the Australian Museum say they favour eucalypt woodland and pine plantations, eat seeds of native trees and pine cones, plus some ground-plant seeds and insects, and nest in a large tree hollow lined with wood chips. BirdLife Australia says the older foods are banksia, hakea and casuarina seeds, and insect larvae in wattle branches, and that Monterey Pine cones are now a major food. Wikipedia's feeding account names Drooping Sheoak (Allocasuarina verticillata), Silver Banksia (Banksia marginata), wattles, and introduced Pinus radiata and a cypress, Cupressus torulosa. Nests are large hollows in tall eucalypts, and roosts are tall emergent eucalypts. Drooping Sheoak, Silver Banksia and several wattles are named for Inverleigh, and River Red Gum and Manna Gum are the local eucalypts. Indexed Leigh News text says sheoak cones are used by cockatoos and parrots, without naming this species. No 5 km record says which tree the birds were feeding in, and pine feeding at Inverleigh is not documented.
yellow-tailed-black-cockatoo.hangouts: Within 5 km of Inverleigh, the Atlas of Living Australia holds 50 records of this species, and no locality string has more than 3. The highest are Hamilton Highway at Native Hut Creek, Murgheboluc (3) and Inverleigh Nature Conservation Reserve (3). Old Shelford Track at Carrah Track, Old Shelford Track between Common Road and Carrah Track, Inverleigh–Winchelsea Road between Thomas Road and Gnarwarre Road, and Lawson Reserve each have 2. Single records include High Street, the Barwon River south of town, and the misspelt Inverleifh Common. The counts are too sparse to name a favourite local spot.
